name: Togo
headline: Togo has a 2019 data law and a patient right to see the file, but records stay on paper or inside each facility.

access.summary: The Public Health Code gives patients the right to see what is in their file, and the 2019 data law gives a right to a copy. A fee up to copying cost is allowed, no deadline is set and there is no portal, so 35.
detail: Article 198 of the Public Health Code (Law 2009-007) says a patient has the right, on request, to the information in their file, and professional secrecy cannot be used against them.
Law 2019-014 (Articles 39 and 40) lets any person get their data in an accessible form, with its origin. A copy must be given on request, but the controller may charge up to the cost of reproduction.

Article 42 lets the patient use this right directly or through a doctor of their choice. The law sets no deadline for answering an access request; a one-month deadline applies only to correction and deletion.
We found no national patient portal. The insurance online services launched in April 2026 handle enrolment, cards and claims, not medical records.

control.summary: Health data may be processed without consent for diagnosis and care under a health professional, and there is no shared record, opt-out or patient-visible access log. The patient's main tool is a general right to object for legitimate reasons.
detail: Article 21 of Law 2019-014 bans processing health data. Article 24 then allows it with consent, but also for care and diagnosis under a professional bound by secrecy, public health, a purpose set by law and crime prevention.
Article 45 lets any person object, for legitimate reasons, to processing of their data. It does not apply when the processing meets a legal obligation.
Article 52 requires controllers to be able to check afterwards who accessed which data and when. This is a duty owed to the regulator, not a log the patient can see.
No national shared record exists, so there is no sharing setting for patients to use.

privacy.summary: Health data is sensitive under Law 2019-014 and fines reach 100 million CFA francs, but the law has no breach notice duty. With no health cases found, this scores the general law; in 2025 the regulator had only its President appointed and logged one complaint.
detail: Law 2019-014 makes health data a sensitive category. Article 71 allows fines up to 100 million CFA francs after a formal notice. Article 86 punishes storing health data without express consent, outside legal cases, with one to five years in prison.
We found no article requiring controllers to notify the regulator or people of a data breach.

Article 57 gives the IPDCP a ten-member board, three named by the President. Its 2025 report says only the President, a gendarmerie officer, has been appointed, and its two directorates are not fully working.
In 2025 the IPDCP recorded 55 declarations, six authorisation requests and one complaint, and reported no fine. In June 2026 it began validating a data protection guide for the health sector.
Togo is outside the EU, so the EHDS does not apply. Article 28 allows transfers abroad only to countries with adequate protection, after an IPDCP opinion.

commercial.summary: Law 2019-014 bans direct marketing without prior consent and lets people refuse, free of charge, the first transfer of their data for prospecting. We found no health-specific rule on data brokers, health apps or de-identified data, and no enforcement.
detail: Article 26 bans direct marketing by any means using a person's data unless they gave prior consent. Article 45 gives a right to be told before data is first passed to third parties for prospecting, and to refuse that free of charge.
Article 24 leaves no general commercial basis for processing health data. Consent or another listed exception is needed.
These are general rules. The IPDCP 2025 report lists eleven declarations from pharmacies and private health services, but no decision on health data sales, consumer apps or de-identified data.

journey.summary: DHIS2 collects aggregate health data, and since April 2026 both insurance funds process claims electronically. There is no national record or exchange; a planned interoperable insurance system was still at the design stage in May 2026.
detail: The Ministry of Health has used DHIS2 since 2016 as its health information system and national data store, also for disease surveillance. It holds aggregate reports, not patient records.

In April 2026 INAM joined CNSS in running an online insurance platform with electronic claims and tracking of each insured person's care: acts, prescriptions and stays. An electronic care sheet linked to facility systems is a future goal.
In May 2026 the ministry held a workshop on SIIG-AMU, a federated system meant to link hospitals, pharmacies, labs and insurers. It noted that a unique patient identifier is still a prerequisite.
A vendor said in 2024 it would build a patient record system for five hospitals for the Global Fund unit. Whether it went live was not verified.

clinical.summary: The law lets clinicians process health data for care, but there is no shared record they can open across providers. A Togolese app founder said patients buy a paper notebook on arrival at hospital and do not come back with the same one.
detail: Article 24(8) of Law 2019-014 allows processing for diagnosis and care under a health professional bound by secrecy. Article 192 of the Public Health Code binds practitioners to professional secrecy.
We found no national system that lets a clinician see notes from another facility. SIIG-AMU, which would exchange data between facilities and insurers, was still being designed in May 2026.
The private app DokitaEyes says it links more than 230 partner facilities through a QR code record seen only by the authorised prescriber. Its co-founder's figures were not verified independently.

research.summary: Health research using personal data needs IPDCP authorisation, and Law 2019-014 punishes research done without telling people their rights or despite their objection. A national ethics committee exists, but no public register of uses was found, so 50.
detail: Article 8 of Law 2019-014 makes processing for health research subject to prior IPDCP authorisation. Article 88 punishes, with up to five years and 25 million CFA francs, research processing without informing each person of their rights, or despite their objection.
Article 436 of the Public Health Code bars drug trials in hospital without informing the ethics committee and forbids experiments without the patient's knowledge.
The Comité de Bioéthique pour la Recherche en Santé (CBRS), based at the Ministry of Health, reviews research protocols, according to the COHRED registry.
We found no public register of research uses. The IPDCP 2025 report says no authorisation request had yet led to a formal authorisation.

ai.summary: Togo has no clinical AI rules. Medical devices are registered under a 2023 ministry service note without expert review bodies, and a national AI strategy was still being prepared in December 2025.
detail: A 2025 review of UEMOA countries found Togo registers class B, C and D devices under a 2023 service note, without the evaluation bodies the UEMOA guidelines call for. It found no functioning national regulatory agency in Togo.
Imports of medicines and medical devices need a registration certificate, handled by the ministry's pharmacy directorate (DPML). We found nothing on software or AI.
In September 2026 the government adopted a decree creating a national medicines and health products agency. Its powers over software were not verified.
In December 2025 Togo First reported a national AI strategy in preparation, focused on public administration, transparency and human oversight.

news.headline: Togo prepares a national strategy on AI in public administration
news.why: Sets direction for AI use, but nothing yet covers AI in clinical care.

news.why: Would be the first step toward records following patients between facilities.
